# Day 4 — Consolidation {#sec-day4-consolidation}

**20 minutes · plenary**

## Say it in one sentence

Fitted on 615 patients and tested on 153 held back, a logistic regression on
glucose alone gives each patient a probability of diabetes; at the default
threshold of 0.5 it correctly classifies 70.6% of them against 64.1% for always
saying "no", and misses 30 of the 55 patients who have the disease.

Every clause in that sentence is load-bearing. Delete the last one and you have
the sentence most published abstracts would have written.

## Self-assessment

- [ ] I can say what changes in a `tidymodels` specification when I swap the
      algorithm, and what changes when I swap the engine.
- [ ] I can state one way in which `LogisticRegression()` and `glm()` are not
      the same model, and the argument that makes them agree.
- [ ] I can convert a probability to odds to log-odds and back, on paper.
- [ ] Given two coefficients and a glucose value, I can produce the predicted
      probability without a computer.
- [ ] I can build a confusion table at a threshold I choose, and name which cell
      a missed diagnosis lands in.
- [ ] I can explain why accuracy rose and sensitivity fell as the threshold went
      up, and which of the two I would report to a diabetes service.

## Questions

1. A colleague reports a classifier with 85% accuracy on a dataset where 85% of
   patients are negative. What have they told you, and what have they not?
2. Two analysts fit "a logistic regression" to the same 50 patients, one in R
   and one in Python, and get coefficients that differ in the first decimal
   place — one of them with the opposite sign. Neither has made a mistake.
   Explain.
3. You lower the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.3. Which of sensitivity,
   specificity, PPV and accuracy are guaranteed to move, which are guaranteed to
   move in a particular direction, and which could go either way?
4. Your model's probabilities are used to decide who is invited for a fasting
   glucose test. The service tells you a missed case is ten times worse than a
   false invitation, not five. Without refitting anything, what do you change
   and roughly where does it end up?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Answers.** (1) They have told you the model is no worse than guessing the
majority class, and nothing else — not whether it finds a single positive case.
Ask for the confusion table. (2) Python's default applies an L2 penalty and R's
`glm()` does not; on 50 rows that is enough to change a small coefficient's sign
(Exercise 4.1). A second, separate cause of a sign flip is the level order of
the outcome factor (Exercise 4.2) — if a student names both, that is the full
answer. (3) Sensitivity cannot fall and specificity cannot rise; PPV usually
falls but is not guaranteed to, because it depends on the mix of the cases you
newly capture; accuracy can go either way and here it falls, from 0.706 to
0.667. (4) Only the threshold. The cost-optimal threshold for a well-calibrated
model is $1/(1 + 10) \approx 0.09$, lower than today's 0.17, so more people are
investigated; on our test set that is close to investigating everybody, which is
the honest answer and worth saying.

**Rubric.** A student has had a good day if they can answer question 1 in two
sentences and question 3 without reaching for the laptop. The ones to worry
about are those who can compute everything on the page and still describe 0.5
as "the" threshold.
:::
:::

## What carries into Day 5

The loose ends left deliberately, each of which opens the next session.

1. We chose a threshold by hand, once, from a cost ratio we invented, and
   scored it on the same 153 rows we chose it on. The threshold-free summary of
   a classifier — the ROC curve and the area under it — is @sec-classification-metrics,
   and so is the question of whether the probabilities deserved to be believed
   in the first place.
2. The random forest in Exercise 4.1 beat the logistic regression by changing
   one line, and nobody could say why it did. @sec-random-forest and @sec-day6
   are that argument.
3. Both scikit-learn's default logistic regression and R's `glmnet` engine
   penalised the coefficients, and we switched the penalty off to make the
   languages agree. Switching it off was the right move for teaching and the
   wrong move for a 50-row dataset. Why a penalty helps, and what it costs, is
   still owed.
